text: THE WHOLE PHILIPPINES LISTENS Architect and political commentator Russell Catapang expressed his support for Vice President Sara Duterte saying that her statements continue to draw attention from Filipinos amid the country's increasingly heated political climate Catapang's statement When VP Sara speaks the whole Philippines listens comes as Duterte has become increasingly vocal in criticizing the Marcos administration particularly over issues involving government performance public services flooding and the difficulties being experienced by ordinary Filipinos In recent statements Duterte has accused the Marcos administration of corruption abuse and political harassment while also speaking about Filipinos struggling with floods and other problems affecting their daily lives On September 12 she called on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr to resign and described him as the problem of the nation Her remarks come amid a deepening political conflict between the Marcos and Duterte camps Duterte is currently facing an impeachment trial and a separate grave-threats case while continuing to reject the accusations and describe some actions against her as political harassment The Palace for its part has maintained that the cases should proceed through due process Against this backdrop Catapang's message appears to emphasize the political weight he believes Duterte's statements carry particularly when she speaks about the concerns and hardships being experienced by Filipinos statenewsonline

Palace Spokesperson Slammed Over Bakit Ka Pa Papasok Kung Trapik Na Remark MANILA Philippines Malacañang Press Officer Claire Castro is facing fresh public anger after telling motorists stuck in the historic NLEX flooding that they simply shouldn't have gone out The remark came during a Palace briefing on the massive gridlock that left thousands of commuters stranded along the North Luzon Expressway amid severe flooding Asked about proposals to suspend toll fees temporarily to ease the situation Castro rejected the idea arguing it would only draw more vehicles onto the road and worsen the congestion Her exact words Bakit ka pa papasok kung trapik na Wag mo na gamitin muna Translation Why even go out if it's already traffic Just don't use it for now The line spread quickly online and for all the wrong reasons Commuters and workers pointed out the obvious most Filipinos don't have the luxury of staying home when floodwaters rise Jobs don't pause for weather Skipping a day at the expressway isn't a real option for someone who loses pay for every hour not worked Castro tried to contain the damage afterward saying her comment was taken out of context She claimed papasok referred literally to entering the expressway itself not to going to work or school The explanation did little to quiet the criticism To many the phrasing read as dismissive of the very real bind stranded workers were in expressway or not This wasn't an isolated moment for Castro Weeks earlier she drew similar backlash after linking teachers to the country's recent spate of school shootings telling reporters that some educators were failing to model good values for students Lawmakers and teacher groups called the remark unfair and beside the point arguing the shootings pointed to failures in gun control and school safety not classroom teaching As with the NLEX comment Castro refused to apologize saying her words had been twisted Two controversies one pattern Each time Castro's remarks have landed on the people already bearing the brunt of a crisis stranded commuters in one case teachers in the other rather than on the institutions responsible for fixing the underlying problems Instead of addressing flood control failures or school safety gaps her comments have shifted blame downward and sparked new backlash for the Palace to manage For an administration already under pressure on both fronts it's another self-inflicted headache one that adds to public frustration rather than resolving it The Green Flag PH Facts First Filipinos Always Question everything Severe Flooding Hits Various Parts of Lipa City as Habagat Brings Persistent Rains Several areas across Lipa City experienced severe flooding as persistent rains brought by the Southwest Monsoon or Habagat enhanced by Typhoon Dolphin international name Persistent rains inundated roads residential communities and commercial areas not only in Lipa but in different parts of the country Photos and videos posted by netizens in the Lipa City Philippines LCP Facebook group showed extensive flooding in various parts of the city with reports coming from Mataas na Lupa Inosloban Marawoy Balintawak San Lucas Sabang B Morada Tibig Pinagkawitan Dagatan and Banay-Banay among other locations Floodwaters affected traffic and movement along the major thoroughfare while several workers were stranded due to unavailability of public vehicles Several posts also sought rescue assistance for people reportedly affected by rising floodwaters including areas around Riles in Balintawak and portions of Inosloban Marawoy and Plaridel These reports underscore the urgency faced by residents in flood-prone communities as water levels rise during prolonged periods of rain For many Lipeños however the latest flooding is more than a weather-related inconvenience It has renewed concerns over the increasing frequency and severity of flooding in areas that were once considered less vulnerable to serious inundation Comments from residents reflected growing frustration with some questioning the effectiveness of the city's urban planning drainage systems and flood-control projects Others pointed to improper garbage disposal and lack of discipline among residents saying that clogged drainage systems can worsen flooding during periods of heavy rain The debate reflects a larger challenge facing a rapidly growing city like Lipa Effective flood management requires properly designed and maintained drainage and waterways responsible urban development regular clearing of obstructions effective solid-waste management and cooperation from both authorities and residents The latest flooding also brings back memories of some of Lipa City's more serious recent flooding events including the widespread flooding associated with Tropical Storm Paeng in October 2022 and Tropical Storm Kristine in October 2024 As rains continue residents are urged to remain vigilant particularly those living and doing business in known flood-prone areas Motorists are likewise encouraged to exercise caution when passing through flooded roads and to avoid attempting to cross areas where the depth or current of floodwater cannot be safely assessed For Lipeños watching the latest developments unfold through community posts in LCP the recurring questions are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore Why is severe flooding becoming more frequent in parts of Lipa City and what long-term measures can finally address it The latest incident serves as another reminder that beyond responding to floods when they happen the city needs to continually examine the underlying causes and strengthen its long-term flood-resilience strategies photos screenshots from various posts in LCP by its members Flooding I have lived in Metro Manila for almost 20 years And every time the rains come the same question returns Why are we still flooding like this Twenty years of different administrations Twenty years of budgets flood-control projects master plans and promises of resilience Yet families still wade through floodwaters Workers are stranded Small businesses lose everything overnight At some point we have to stop calling this merely a problem of weather A country exposed to 20 typhoons per year should have spent decades becoming one of the best-prepared nations on Earth Instead we have normalized dysfunction We celebrate rescue when we should demand prevention We praise relief operations when we should demand systems that work We applaud politicians wading through floodwaters when the true measure of leadership is how many Filipinos no longer have to Leadership is drainage that works Waterways that are maintained Cities planned beyond the next election Public transportation that works Budgets that produce results Leaders held accountable The Philippines does not lack talent resources ingenuity or hardworking people What we have lacked for far too long is leadership that builds institutions instead of endlessly managing crises So where is the hope Not in waiting for the next politician to save us Hope is raising the standard of what Filipinos are willing to accept After almost 20 years in Manila I still believe in this country But loving the Philippines should never require pretending everything is okay Sometimes hope begins by refusing to accept what should never have become normal

TYPHOON PEDRING NESAT DEVASTATED METRO MANILA CENTRAL AND NORTHERN LUZON On This Day September 27 2011 Typhoon Pedring PH International Name NESAT carved a path of catastrophic destruction across the Philippines when it made landfall on September 27 2011 As a powerful Category 4 equivalent typhoon it unleashed ferocious maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h and dropped torrents of relentless rain that quickly overwhelmed Luzon The immense storm triggered widespread landslips brought down vital electrical grids and forced hundreds of thousands of residents to abandon their homes for safety The sheer volume of water forced major dams to open their spillway gates significantly aggravating the downstream flooding in neighboring northern provinces In Metro Manila the storm brought the nation's capital to a complete standstill evoking terrifying memories of Tropical Storm Ondoy PH from two years prior Strong gales combined with an exceptionally high storm surge generated massive 20 foot waves that breached the historic seawall along Roxas Boulevard The resulting saltwater deluge swamped key arterial roads the United States Embassy and the iconic five-star Sofitel Philippine Plaza hotel Meanwhile low lying sectors like Marikina experienced critical flooding as local rivers swelled to dangerous levels trapping families on rooftops and necessitating emergency rubber boat rescues The aftermath of Typhoon PEDRING left behind a staggering socioeconomic toll claiming 85 lives in the Philippines alone and leaving billions of pesos in property damage Central and Northern Luzon's expansive agricultural fields-the backbone of the country's rice supply suffered heavily with massive swathes of crops entirely wiped out by the standing floodwaters Compounding the humanitarian crisis communities like Calumpit and Hagonoy in Bulacan remained submerged in chest-deep water for days without clean electricity or drinking water The disaster forced a declaration of a state of calamity across Luzon marking PEDRING as one of the most economically devastating typhoons of its time Philippine Weather Disturbances 27 September 2026 Pedring2011 Typhoon Pedring NESAT2011 Typhoon THE RAIN IS NATURAL THE SUFFERING ISN'T Metro Manila is flooding again today Roads in several cities have been flooded some becoming impassable while La Mesa Dam reached spilling level and residents along the Tullahan River were told to evacuate And we hear a familiar explanation The rain was simply too strong Climate change is real The weather is becoming more extreme Nature cannot be controlled All of that is true But it can also become a very convenient excuse Government cannot stop the rain It can decide whether drainage systems work whether waterways are kept clear whether pumping stations are maintained whether watersheds are protected and whether billions spent on flood control actually produce flood control The President himself acknowledged that some flood-control projects in Bulacan were never built His administration is still investigating projects alleged to be ghost substandard or ineffective So yes blame the rain for falling But don't blame the rain for money disappearing Don't blame climate change for a ghost project Don't blame nature for poor planning And don't ask people standing in waist-deep water to accept government failure as an act of God Other countries face nature too Singapore lives with intense tropical rainfall In the 1960s and 1970s it suffered widespread flooding Decades of drainage expansion detention systems strict building rules maintenance and careful planning reduced its officially identified flood-prone area from around 3,200 hectares to less than 30 hectares today Japan cannot prevent earthquakes Yet it prepares buildings infrastructure evacuation systems and communities for them Around Tokyo Japan built one of the world's largest underground flood channels to divert overflowing rivers and reduce flood damage They did not defeat nature They prepared for it We have not lacked money in our country We have spent enormous sums on flood-control projects Yet we are now dealing with a major corruption scandal involving precisely those projects People pay taxes for protection from floods Money is allocated for that protection Then the rains come and families lose appliances cars businesses school days Lives And afterward they are told Malakas kasi ang ulan Of course the rain was strong That was the reason to prepare No serious engineer can promise a flood-free Metro Manila Even Singapore still experiences flash floods Climate change is making the problem harder The proper measure of government is whether flooding becomes less frequent less deep shorter more predictable and less deadly That requires drainage maps watershed management zoning enforcement retention basins sewer maintenance pumping capacity garbage collection engineering standards long-term budgets and COMPETENT people allowed to do their jobs It also requires public money actually reaching the project for which it was intended Nature will always test a country The rain will fall on an honest government and a corrupt government alike The difference is what happens after the rain reaches the ground If another generation of Filipinos is still wading through the same streets after billions more have been spent we should ask what exactly our leaders have been building while the rest of the Filipinos were paying for it Teach Better

The Silver Lining or the Endless Storm A Critical Look at Flood Response in the Philippines By Dr Tony Leachon The Philippines visited by 20-25 typhoons a year lives in a perpetual cycle of disaster Every two weeks another storm arrives bringing floods displacement and disease Hospitals brace for leptospirosis outbreaks highways choke with traffic and families line up for financial assistance President Ferdinand Marcos Jr s recent meeting with Cabinet members and agencies highlights the government's intent search and rescue evacuation financial aid hospital preparedness and infrastructure repair On paper these are necessary steps But the critical question remains is this enough or are we trapped in reactive governance Critical Analysis What went wrong Flood control projects remain unfinished or poorly maintained Waste management failures clog drainage systems amplifying floods Hospital surge capacity is reactive not preventive Financial aid is short-term relief not systemic reform What will go wrong Rising climate intensity will overwhelm outdated infrastructure Leptospirosis and dengue will swamp hospitals beyond capacity Economic losses from repeated floods will erode national productivity Public trust will weaken if governance remains focused only on band-aid solutions The silver lining The frequency of disasters forces resilience and innovation Communities develop solidarity and adaptive practices International models Japan Singapore Netherlands offer proven strategies for flood control and waste management The crisis creates political pressure for systemic reform a chance to finally institutionalize prevention The Question Still Stands Yes the question is still valid What choices do we have But the answer cannot remain in the cycle of rescue relief and repair The choice must shift toward prevention resilience and governance reform Path Forward National Flood Control Act anchored on science not patronage Waste-to-energy programs to unclog waterways and generate power Hospital surge systems with pre-positioned supplies and modular ICUs Community resilience education to empower barangays beyond relief dependence Closing Reflection The Philippines cannot stop typhoons But it can stop being overwhelmed by them The silver lining lies not in the storms themselves but in the opportunity to transform crisis into reform If we continue to ask what went wrong without acting the answer will always be the same floods disease and despair But if we ask what can we build now then perhaps the endless storm can finally give way to a future of resilience Tony Leachon

DOST PAGASA inaugurates JICA funded CDO River Basin Flood Forecasting and Warning System DOST-PAGASA has inaugurated the Cagayan De Oro River Basin Flood Forecasting and Warning System FFWS today at the PAGASA Mindanao Regional Services Division in El Salvador City Misamis Oriental This facility aims to provide early warning and real-time monitoring for flood-prone communities in Misamis Oriental and some parts of Bukidnon enhancing disaster preparedness in the region Funded by the Government of Japan through the Japan International Cooperation Agency JICA this system features an enhanced flood forecasting and warning including additional telemetered and sturdier rainfall and water level monitoring stations along with X-Band radars These strategically positioned stations spanning from the upstream to downstream sections of the river basin will enable hydrologists at the CDORBFFWS to provide accurate timely and relevant flood bulletins and warnings to communities vulnerable to flooding DOST officials graced the event with Secretary Renato U Solidum Jr as the inaugural speaker Also in support and attendance are DOST Undersecretary for Regional Operations Engr Sancho A Mabborang and PAGASA Administrator Dr Nathaniel T Servando Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Japan His Excellency Kazuya Endo and Senior Representative of JICA Mr Morishima Takanori also attended the event delivering messages of support Local Chief Executives and representatives of involved LGUs partner agencies stakeholders and many officials also gathered for the inauguration receiving plaques of appreciation The launching event featured a blessing ceremony unveiling of the marker ribbon-cutting facility tour and a press conference CDO River Basin One DOST4U Science For The People PAGASA Flood Warning DOST Bukidnon DOST Camiguin DOST Lanao del Norte DOST Misamis Occidental DOST Misamis Oriental

THE BLUEPRINT FOR FLOOD CONTROL MASTERPLAN IS READY The recent post by FB page More of Davao has reignited an important conversation-Davao City's flooding problem is not due to the absence of a plan In fact one already exists The Japan International Cooperation Agency JICA in partnership with the Department of Public Works and Highways DPWH completed the Project for Master Plan and Feasibility Study on Flood Control and Drainage in Davao City in July 2023 after several years of technical studies and consultations The project itself commenced in November 2018 following the signing of the Record of Discussions in April 2018 between JICA and the Philippine government The completed master plan is comprehensive It covers the Davao Matina and Talomo River Basins and recommends a combination of structural measures including river dredging cut-off channels retarding ponds retarding basins and drainage improvements to significantly reduce flood risks in the city These are not theoretical concepts They are the product of years of hydrological studies engineering surveys and technical analysis by Filipino and Japanese experts This is why the public deserves to know one thing what is the current status of implementation Large Official Development Assistance ODA infrastructure projects commonly undergo additional stages that include financing arrangements detailed engineering environmental compliance right-of-way acquisition and government approvals before actual construction begins That does not diminish the urgency Every flooding incident reminds us that studies alone cannot protect lives Master plans only become meaningful once construction begins The engineering has already been completed The science has already been established The blueprint already exists The next chapter should no longer be about producing another report It should be about turning years of planning into flood control infrastructure that protects communities businesses and lives Because when it comes to flooding what Davaoeños need most is not another promise-they need progress backed by action

Flood in Obrero 1960s I am taking a quick break from my work Speaking of the heavy flood it reminds me of something Here is a photo of some residents in Obrero at the corner of Clarin and Porras Streets during the flood This photo comes from the contributor's grandmother's family album The scene was possibly taken in the 1960s We learn from historian Antonio Figueroa that Barrio Obrero had its beginnings in the pre-Commonwealth period The idea was to set aside parcels of land to be developed into villages for working men And let me tell you a collective memory from my personal journal about Obrero's surrounding areas In old maps of Davao the area from Trading Boulevard Sta Ana Agdao all the way to Obrero was a swampy or marshy and mangrove area In fact in Ubalde and R Castillo roads there were plenty of Pagatpat trees At high tide seawater would come in bringing with it fish like ibis bugaong wild tilapia and the water snake called tangkig Of course there were also crabs like kuray katang and alimango In Obrero alone sometime in the past some college students who stayed in boarding houses fondly recalled how they would put their shoes in a basin floating in dirty water so they could wear them the next morning I wonder how many parts of the city have still experienced flooding since the 1960s or even earlier I want to learn from urban planners And the two young men from the right They are so wet in the rain Neil Teves Author's note Photo courtesy of the Bonifacio and Ermitania Delute Family Albums Contributed by Neil Gementiza Photo first posted by Paul Corpus on November 2 2019 for educational purposes

THE HOSTAGE BLUEPRINT JICA MASTERPLAN FOR DAVAO CITY What if I told you that a blueprint to stop the flooding in Davao City is already finished It was designed by some of the best engineers in the world printed and is currently sitting on a desk in Manila Here is the truth about the JICA Master Plan the political war currently holding it hostage and what our Local Government Unit LGU is doing to keep our heads above water while we wait The Real Solution The JICA Master Plan Back in 2018 the Philippine government partnered with the Japan International Cooperation Agency JICA to solve our city's flooding Instead of just building basic concrete walls which easily overflow the Japanese and local engineers designed a massive city-wide system The core of the plan involves digging massive retarding basins giant empty catch-ponds built in the uplands When a storm hits millions of gallons of water would flow into these basins and be held there safely trapping the water before it ever reaches barangays like Ma-a Matina and Talomo It is brilliant it is proven and it is ready But just look at the timeline of how it got stuck in politics Here is the timeline April 2019 THE STUDY BEGINS The Philippine government and the Japan International Cooperation Agency JICA sign an agreement to create a long-term multi-basin master plan 2018-2022 WHY WASN'T IT BUILT UNDER DUTERTE A common question is why this wasn't funded during former President Rodrigo Duterte's term The answer is engineering reality The Japanese engineers were still studying our rivers You cannot fund or construct a mega-project when the architects haven't finished the blueprints July 2023 THE BLUEPRINT IS FINISHED JICA officially completes the Master Plan Instead of basic walls it proposes PHP 41.7 Billion to build massive retarding basins giant empty bowls upstream to catch and hold storm water before it hits our urban barangays AUGUST 9 2024 VP SARA CALLS OUT THE MISSING BUDGET Vice President Sara Duterte issues a strong public statement pointing out the lack of government action She calls out the current administration for refusing to fund the finalized master plan questioning if the budget is being intentionally withheld simply because the sitting mayor is a Duterte Baka naman may alinlangan pa hinggil dito dahil Duterte ang mayor at mas mamarapatin nilang gibain na lang she stated 2025 Present STILL WAITING FOR FUNDS Despite the blueprint being ready for over two years the national government has still not released the funding needed to actually build it Bureaucracy or Sabotage While politicians debate whether the delay is just standard government red tape for a foreign loan or a deliberate political attack to damage the Duterte family ordinary Davaoeños are the collateral damage We are the ones sweeping mud out of our homes The ultimate solution to our flooding is being treated as a political football What is the LGU Doing While We Wait The Davao City local government cannot afford a PHP 41.7 Billion mega-project on its own They cannot single-handedly buy multi-hectare lands to build giant retarding ponds without national funding However they are not just sitting around waiting for our government Without the big blueprint the LGU is focusing heavily on immediate urban drainage nature-based mitigation and survival Here is what the city is doing right now Aggressive Drainage and Inlet Upgrades The City Engineer's Office CEO and Task Force Drainage are continuously ripping up flood-prone choke points In 2025 alone they funded five new major inlet projects to help water subside faster on critical roads like Diversion Road fronting Panacan Cemetery Quezon Boulevard and Cabantian-Bunawan Preventing Blockages The city's Ancillary Services Unit ASU is conducting aggressive year-round desilting and garbage clearing of these new drainage systems so the street-level water actually has somewhere to go Smart Early Warning Systems If the LGU cannot completely stop the water they focus on keeping people alive Davao City relies heavily on its high-definition river cameras monitoring the Talomo Matina and Davao rivers 24/7 This real-time Time to act AGUSAN BASIN DAVAO FLOODS SIGNS OF IMPENDING DISASTER By Manny Piñol In October of 2016 President Rody Duterte visited the typhoon devastated Cagayan Valley Region he warned that unless the mighty Cagayan River is dredged soon a disaster could happen inn the low-lying towns along the country's longest river The President said that soil erosion in the denuded mountains of the region ravaged by illegal logging operations have resulted in the heavy siltation of the meandering river causing it to overflow every time the rainy season or typhoons come The President's grim warning came true last week not in Cagayan Valley but at least five areas in Mindanao where soil erosion from bald mountains have caused heavy siltation and flash floods Flash floods and inundations occurred in Cagayan de Oro and Misamis Oriental Bukidnon the Cotabato River Basin Davao Region and the Agusan River Basin As heavy rains brought by the Tail-End of the Cold Front TECF poured in the mountains of these areas floodwaters rushed down causing rivers to overflow destroying crops and properties Hardest hit was the Agusan River Basin area which stretches from the mountains of Davao where mining and logging operations destroyed the forest cover to Butuan City up north Floods turned thousands of hectares of farmlands into a virtual sea affecting thousands of farming families When I visited the flood-hit areas and consulted with local leaders Thursday and Friday local leaders and stakeholders agreed that unless something is done fast a disaster worse than what these areas are suffering from DAVAO'S FLOOD DEFENSES EXPLAINED How Retarding Ponds Cut-Off Channels and Dredging Work When millions of cubic meters of water pour down from upstream mountain catchments into the Davao Talomo and Matina River Basins how do we protect our communities from being submerged The insights and data shared here are not my own-they are drawn directly from the official DPWH-JICA Flood Control Master Plan In Part 1 we broke down why different neighborhoods face completely different flood risks Today in PART 2 we take a deep dive into the 4 major hard engineering solutions designed under this master plan to store accelerate and safely convey extreme 100 year flood waters out to sea 1 PRIORITY RETARDING PONDS Temporary Storage Upstream Affected Downstream Areas Callawa Mandug Waan Tigatto Ma-a Bucana Talomo Proper Matina Crossing and Matina Aplaya How It Works Think of these as massive engineered overflow reservoirs During heavy storms river channels quickly fill up Retarding ponds capture the peak flood surge upstream holding the excess water back until river levels safely drop The Engineering Specs Davao River RP 08 Callawa New Valencia 3.5 Million m3 capacity Davao River RP 09 Upper Callawa Bend 2.1 Million m3 capacity Davao River RP 11 Mandug New Carmen 4.8 Million m3 capacity Talomo River Basin Multi-site retention ponds covering approximately 4.8 million m2 to absorb excess volume before it hits downtown Matina River Basin A network of 12 critical offline/online ponds Ponds 8-10 13-18 23-25 strategically distributed to capture and cut peak flood discharge by 200 m3 s Combined Impact Over 10.4 MILLION cubic meters of temporary flood storage for the Davao River alone plus massive secondary retention across Talomo and Matina-the equivalent of thousands of Olympic-sized swimming pools held back from swamping the city 2 CUT-OFF CHANNELS COC Straightening Extreme River Bends Affected Areas Callawa New Valencia Ma-a Riverfront Area plus localized bottlenecks in Matina and Talomo How It Works Natural winding river loops slow down water velocity forcing floodwaters to pile up and breach their banks Cut-off channels construct straight bypass canals directly across narrow meander necks The Engineering Specs The 1.8 km Callawa Cut-Off Channel speeds up water flow dramatically dropping peak flood levels upstream and relieving severe hydraulic pressure on tight river bends Additionally short-term cut-off channel works are programmed for the winding sections of the Matina and Talomo rivers to prevent backwater piling and safely accelerate flow toward the coast 3 CHANNEL WIDENING and DREDGING Reclaiming River Capacity Affected Areas Ma-a Tigatto Bankerohan Barangay 19 Bucana Matina Crossing and Talomo Urban Center How It Works Decades of mountain erosion have washed tons of silt onto the riverbed choking its flow capacity while dense urban build-up has dangerously narrowed the natural waterways The Engineering Specs Deep channel dredging and excavation along critical downstream reaches of the Davao River lower the riverbed profile-expanding cross-sectional flow area so the river can carry higher discharge volumes In the Matina River the channel will be physically widened by an average of 6 meters 3m on each bank and 6 restrictive hydraulic bottleneck bridges will be replaced This massive upgrade will more than double Matina's flow capacity from a dangerous 150 m3 s up to a safe 350 m3 s 4 FLOODWALLS DIKES and REVETMENTS Wall-to-Wall Protection Affected Areas Densely populated urban barangays along the Davao Talomo and Matina river corridors How It Works Where urban density prevents widening the river lateral structures contain the water within the channel Raised concrete dikes prevent overflow while heavy reinforced concrete revetments absorb raging currents to prevent riverbank collapse The Engineering Specs Alongside the massive dikes for the main Davao River and drainage integration at the MacArthur Highway corridor in Talomo the highly vulnerable Matina River urban stretch will receive heavy reinforcements New concrete floodwalls here will average 2.6 meters high-reaching up to a towering 5.4 meters in critical spots including freeboard to securely contain the raging 100 year flood volumes THE TAKEAWAY SYSTEM INTEGRATION IS KEY No single dike or dredging project can solve Davao City's flood challenges alone Retarding ponds hold back the surge upstream Cut-Off Channels speed up flow past tight meanders and downstream widening dredging and dikes safely guide the water out to the Davao Gulf DAVAO FLOOD CONTROL SERIES 4 PART DEEP DIVE Read Part 1 Davao Flood Map Explained PART 2 Hard Engineering Interventions You Are Here NEXT UP PART 3 Non-Structural Measures Early text: IT WAS MORE THAN A PUNCH By Truth Stream The rain did not arrive with a warning loud enough to stir panic It came like countless other rainy nights in Davao City Steady familiar almost ordinary Dabawenyos tucked their children into bed believing morning would come as it always had But somewhere in the darkness the waters were already gathering strength silently preparing to rewrite the lives of an entire community Before dawn broke on June 30 2011 Matina Pangi had become the epicenter of one of Davao City's deadliest flash floods In a matter of minutes homes were swallowed by a raging torrent Parents desperately searched for their children Neighbors risked their own lives to save strangers When the floodwaters finally receded they left behind more than shattered houses and mud-covered streets They left empty cradles unfinished dreams and a city mourning the loss of more than thirty lives most of them children Mayor Inday Sara Duterte then only 33 years old and herself a young mother woke up to a city devastated by tragedy One infant was never found Entire families were caught in total darkness as floodwaters engulfed their homes Some survived only by climbing trees while others escaped to the Matina Pangi Bridge carrying nothing but the clothes on their backs and the cellphones they managed to save As daylight broke the full extent of the catastrophe emerged lifeless bodies waiting to be recovered children still missing families desperately searching for loved ones and survivors left with nothing but mud where their homes once stood For Mayor Sara there was no time to grieve She immediately led relief operations visited evacuation centers comforted bereaved families and coordinated rescue and emergency response efforts Sleep and rest had to wait Yet before the city could even begin to recover from one tragedy another crisis erupted A court-ordered demolition in Agdao was set to proceed despite the city's standing policy that no demolition should take place unless affected residents had first been relocated Knowing the emotional state of the people after the flash flood Mayor Sara appealed to the court sheriff for just one or two hours so she could personally speak with the residents Her request was neither unreasonable nor defiant She simply wanted to prevent panic violence and the possibility of more people getting hurt Barely twenty-four hours had passed since more than thirty lives most of them children had been lost She did not want another tragedy unfolding in another part of the city Her plea was ignored While she was still in Matina attending to flood victims she learned that the demolition had already begun She rushed to Agdao wearing a light blue shirt and her signature short hair where television cameras were already rolling She motioned for the sheriff to come closer Seconds later she threw the punch that would become one of the most replayed political images in recent Philippine history Across the country many saw only a mayor punching a court officer What many never saw was the context he grief exhaustion and emotional weight of the previous twenty-four hours They did not see the flood victims she had just come from the parents searching for missing children or the families she had spent the day consoling The image of the punch became the story while everything that led to it slowly faded from public memory Mayor Sara later ensured that the sheriff received medical treatment publicly expressed regret over what had happened and in time both of them moved on from the incident Fifteen years later however that single moment was once again thrust into the national spotlight during the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte where prosecutors cited it as evidence of an alleged pattern of violent behavior For many Dabawenyos though the hearing revived a different memory They remembered the flood before they remembered the punch They remembered the children who died the families who lost everything and the young mayor who spent every waking hour responding to one of the darkest days in the city's history before rushing to stop what she believed could become another human tragedy As old footage resurfaced so did countless personal stories from Dabawenyos whose admiration for the Dutertes had been shaped not by political slogans but by lived experience Whether one agrees with Sara Duterte's actions that day or not history is rarely captured in a single frame Sometimes what appears to be a single punch is only the final chapter of a much longer story One written in floodwaters grief impossible decisions and a leader's fierce determination to stand with her people Perhaps that is why fifteen years later Dabawenyos continue to tell the story differently They remember not only the punch They remember everything that came before it VP Sara Duterte Impeachment Trial vpsaraimpeach
